title: Caller Diligence
explain: When my service calls a third party, I am the one who has to behave. I ask six questions about every outbound call: how I avoid storming it, how I time-box the call, what I do on errors, what I do when the response is wrong, how I undo earlier steps if the failure is critical, and what I do when it keeps failing. Each has a standard mechanism.
model:
Six questions, six mechanisms (think of them as layers around one call):

| # | Question | Mechanism |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | Not storm it | per-host [connection pool](#/sd/f/connection-pooling) + client-side [rate limiter](#/sd/f/rate-limiter) matching its quota + [concurrency limiter](#/sd/f/concurrency-limiter) |
| 2 | Time-gate each request | per-request [timeout](#/sd/f/timeout), shorter than your caller's deadline |
| 3 | Exceptions | classify: retry timeouts, 429, 503 with [backoff and jitter](#/sd/f/backoff-jitter); don't retry validation 4xx; idempotent writes |
| 4 | Invalid response or data mismatch | **output adapter** (anti-corruption layer): validate schema, map fields and enums, quarantine bad payloads |
| 5 | Critical failure needs a revert | **saga**: compensating actions in reverse order |
| 6 | It keeps failing | [circuit breaker](#/sd/f/circuit-breaker) + backoff and jitter on recovery |

**Layering for one attempt:** breaker check, rate-limit token and concurrency slot, connection from the pool, request with timeout, then the adapter; retry wraps this, and the saga is the business-level escape hatch. Retries multiply load, so every attempt, not just the first, passes the limiters, and an open breaker stops attempts altogether.

details.q: The vendor returns HTTP 200 with `{"status": "OK", "amount": null}` and your ledger code crashes. Which mechanism is for this?
details.a: The output adapter. The call succeeded at transport level but the data is wrong; validating and mapping at the boundary keeps vendor quirks out of your domain and quarantines payloads that fail the contract. Retries and breakers address availability, not shape.

details.q: Checkout reserves inventory, charges a card, then asks a shipping vendor for a label, which fails permanently. What about the earlier steps?
details.a: Run compensating actions in reverse as a saga: void or refund the charge, release inventory. There is no distributed rollback across services, so every step needs an explicit compensation, and the compensations must themselves be idempotent and retryable.

details.q: A vendor returns 503 to everything; 2,000 callers retry three times immediately with 30 s timeouts. Someone proposes 60 s timeouts. Better?
details.a: No. Longer waits and immediate retries amplify load on a service that is already down and tie up your threads. Open a circuit breaker after repeated failures, fail fast, and probe with exponential backoff and jitter after it half-opens.

details.q: What is the longest a call can take with 3 attempts of 2 s timeout, waiting 0.5 s then 1 s between attempts?
details.a: 3 x 2 s + 0.5 + 1 = 7.5 s. If your own caller has a shorter deadline, derive the retry budget from it instead of choosing it independently, or the work continues after nobody is listening.

Timeouts, connection errors, 429 (honouring `Retry-After`) and 503. Not 400-style validation errors or permanent 4xx: the same request will fail again. Writes are retried only with an [idempotency key](#/sd/f/idempotency).

details.q: In what order do the guards sit around one attempt?
details.a: Breaker first (fail fast before spending quota), then a rate-limit token and a concurrency slot, then a connection from the pool, then the request with timeout, then the adapter on the response. Limits come before the connection so storms are stopped at the source.

details.q: Why do limiters and the pool matter if the vendor has its own rate limiting?
details.a: Their limit is a punishment, yours is courtesy and protection: hitting 429s wastes your own budget and can extend penalties. Match your client-side limit to the contract and shape the traffic before it leaves.

prompts.q: List the six caller-diligence questions and a mechanism for each.
points: Not storming: pool, rate limiter, concurrency limiter
Exceptions: classify, backoff and jitter, idempotent writes
Critical failure revert: saga with compensations
Persistent failure: circuit breaker plus backoff and jitter

prompts.q: Draw the layers around a single outbound call to a payment vendor.
points: Pooled connection, timeout on the request
Retries re-enter the limiters; saga for business rollback

prompts.q: The vendor starts failing under load. What do you do, and what do you avoid?
points: Exponential backoff with jitter when probing
Avoid immediate retries and longer timeouts
Retry budget derived from the caller's deadline
